raw_case_text:
A 49-years-old male presented to the emergency department (ED) with a history of intermittent fever and abdominal pain for one week. He had a history of diabetes mellitus (DM) (HbA1c was 7.2% on oral hypoglycemic medications) and coronary artery disease. One year earlier, he underwent cardiac surgery for mitral valve fibroelastoma resection and coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). There was no history of smoking, alcohol intake, or substance abuse. On examination, he was afebrile initially, and other vital signs were within the normal range. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the left upper quadrant without guarding or rigidity. Examination of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems was unremarkable. Laboratory results were significant for normocytic anemia (hemoglobin was 10.9 g/dL) and elevated C-reactive protein level (147.5 mg/L), but normal renal and liver functions parameters. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed a wedge-shaped hypodense lesion in the spleen suggestive of splenic infarction [Fig. 1A]. Echocardiography (echo) revealed moderate aortic regurgitation and a rounded mass measuring approximately 1.5 by 1 cm attached to the left aortic valve coronary cusp, which was not present in the previous echo one year earlier [Fig. 2]. The patient was initiated on empirical antimicrobial therapy. As the patient continued to be febrile in the initial days of hospital admission and blood cultures did not grow any organisms, the antibiotics coverage was escalated to cefepime and vancomycin.
After six days of admission, he developed acute chest pain associated with severe breathlessness. He was tachypneic and tachycardic; he was desaturated to 90%; chest examination revealed bilateral crepitation, so immediate medical management for acute pulmonary congestion was initiated with intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside infusion, and non-invasive ventilation. As his respiratory parameters did not show significant improvement, he was electively intubated. Repeated echo showed severe aortic regurgitation with normal ejection fraction. A decision was made for surgical intervention, and surgical aortic valve replacement was done. Intraoperative findings included the presence of abscess formation at the aortic valve annulus and aortic wall at the level of the sinus-tubular junction, in addition to the destruction of the left coronary leaflet. The mitral valve leaflets were normal in appearance.
Postoperatively, clinical examination revealed unequal pupils and cold extremities. CT brain showed multiple brain hypodensities, suggesting thrombo-embolic stroke [Fig. 2B]. CT aortogram demonstrated saddle thrombus at the aortic bifurcation occluding the proximal parts of common iliac arteries [Fig. 2C]. Subsequently, emergency laparotomy was carried on with successful removal of aortic thrombus, and hemicolectomy was performed due to the presence of gangrenous bowel. On day nine, the fungal stain was positive from the tissue culture of the aortic valve; hence, amphotericin B was added to the antimicrobial regimen. However, the patient's clinical condition deteriorated, and he developed septic shock and multiorgan failure. Unfortunately, on day 11 of admission, the patient had a cardiac arrest and passed away. The following day after the patient's death, the fungal culture of the aortic valve mass revealed A. flavus.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old diabetic male presented 1 year after mitral valve fibroelastoma resection and coronary artery bypass grafting with a 1-week history of intermittent fever and left upper quadrant abdominal pain, followed on hospital day 6 by acute chest pain and severe dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One year after undergoing open cardiac surgery (mitral valve fibroelastoma resection and CABG), the patient presented to the emergency department with 1 week of intermittent fever and left upper quadrant abdominal pain due to a splenic infarction and a 1.5 x 1 cm aortic valve mass. Despite empirical antibiotics (escalated to cefepime and vancomycin) with negative blood cultures, his fever persisted and on hospital day 6 he developed acute chest pain, severe pulmonary edema, and acute severe aortic regurgitation requiring emergency surgical aortic valve replacement, complicated postoperatively by thromboembolic strokes and a saddle aortoiliac occlusion with bowel gangrene.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mitral valve papillary fibroelastoma resection and coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) 1 year prior; type 2 diabetes mellitus on oral hypoglycemics (HbA1c 7.2%); coronary artery disease; non-smoker, non-drinker, no illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1-week intermittent fever, left upper quadrant abdominal pain, and on hospital day 6 acute chest pain and severe orthopnea/dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam: afebrile with normal vitals, left upper quadrant abdominal tenderness without guarding, and unremarkable cardiopulmonary exam. Day 6 acute decompensation: tachypneic, tachycardic, SpO2 90%, and bilateral pulmonary crepitations requiring intubation. Immediate postoperative exam after AVR: anisocoria (unequal pupils) and cold lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL), elevated CRP (147.5 mg/L), HbA1c 7.2%, and normal renal and liver function tests. Serial peripheral blood cultures were negative. Admission echocardiography showed a new 1.5 x 1.0 cm rounded vegetation on the left coronary cusp of the aortic valve with moderate aortic regurgitation, which progressed on day 6 repeat echocardiography to severe aortic regurgitation with preserved LVEF.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission abdominal CT demonstrated a wedge-shaped splenic infarction. Intraoperative exploration during day 6 surgical aortic valve replacement revealed destruction of the left coronary cusp and an abscess involving the aortic annulus and sinotubular junction aortic wall (normal mitral valve). Postoperative head CT demonstrated multifocal thromboembolic cerebral infarctions, and CT aortography revealed a saddle fungal thromboembolus at the aortic bifurcation occluding the bilateral proximal common iliac arteries with gangrenous colon on emergency laparotomy. Fungal staining of the excised aortic valve tissue turned positive on hospital day 9, and fungal culture isolated Aspergillus flavus on day 12 (1 day postmortem).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fatal blood-culture-negative native aortic valve Aspergillus flavus infective endocarditis with annular abscess occurring 1 year after prior cardiac surgery, complicated by embolic splenic infarction, acute severe aortic regurgitation, multifocal cerebral thromboembolism, and a saddle aortoiliac mycotic thrombus causing colonic gangrene, definitively confirmed by excised aortic valve fungal microscopy and culture growing A. flavus. Despite emergency surgical aortic valve replacement, emergency laparotomy with aortoiliac thromboembolectomy and hemicolectomy, and addition of intravenous amphotericin B on hospital day 9, the patient progressed to refractory septic shock, multiorgan failure, and fatal cardiac arrest on hospital day 11.
